Senses.Explanation: Bian He is the pre-Chan jade-bearer whom the corpus invokes through the uncut-jade story. The name occurs 90 times in 52 allowlisted texts. In his Book of Serenity commentary, Wansong Xingxiu retells the defining event: Bian He found an uncut stone in a valley of Mount Jing, offered it to King Li of Chu, was told it was stone, and had one foot cut off. Chan interviews compress the story into answers such as “white jade without flaw; Bian He has his foot cut off” (白玉無瑕，卞和刖足). A student explicitly adopts the role by telling Touzi Datong, “I bring you the uncut jade and ask you to carve and polish it”; when Touzi Datong refuses it as beam material, the student says, “then Bian He has nowhere to emerge” (卞和無出身處). Yuanwu’s verse names the repeated offering and its cost: “laughable, Bian He presents the jade three times; even if honored, both feet are cut off” (卞和三獻玉，縱榮刖却一雙足). Danxia Zichun's verse draws its own comparison: “Mount Jing’s fine jade—why discern it? … Bian He had knowledge; the king of Chu rejected him” (卞和有智楚王嫌). Zen therefore deploys Bian He as the named bearer of unrecognized jade in answers, student self-comparison, verses, and case commentary. These records, not a general literary biography, define the entry.

Senses.Explanation: To hear a sound and awaken to the Way is a recurrent formula paired with seeing a form and clarifying mind. Yunmen raises the paired formula as a question rather than a procedure. Other masters repeat it in hall addresses and public exchanges. The corpus also refuses automatic endorsement: Tian’an Sheng compares it to quenching thirst by imagining plums, and Fuyan Baozong says it loses Guanyin’s eye. Zen bends the formula into something to test, challenge, or reject in encounter. Hearing a sound is not presented here as a guaranteed staged procedure.

Senses.Explanation: Not mind, not buddha: a recorded saying, answer, question, and the second member of the sequence beginning with 'this mind is this buddha' (即心即佛). The exact negative wording is (非心非佛). In the Mazu exchange, an unnamed monk asks why Mazu says 'this mind is this buddha'; Mazu Daoyi answers, 'to stop a small child crying' (為止小兒啼). Asked, 'What about when the crying stops?' (啼止時如何), he replies, 'not mind, not buddha' (非心非佛). Funiu Zizai explicitly classifies the pair: 'This mind is this buddha is a sentence seeking medicine where there is no illness; not mind, not buddha is a sentence countering medicine and illness' (即心即佛是無病求藥句，非心非佛是藥病對治句). Other records set it beside a longer 'not mind, not buddha, not a thing' expression, ask 'What is not mind, not buddha?' (如何是非心非佛), or treat it as a question answered with another recorded saying—Heshan Wuyin answers, 'Heshan knows how to beat the drum' (禾山解打鼓). Damei Fachang's case preserves an explicit contrast: told that Mazu now says 'not mind, not buddha,' Damei answers that he still keeps 'this mind is this buddha.' Zen bends a bare double negation into a mobile public-interview saying whose recorded force depends on its speaker, sequence, and answer rather than an imported abstract definition. Yuanwu Keqin tells the assembly to set ‘not mind, not buddha’ to one side; Songyuan Chongyue raises Mazu's paired sayings and asks whether they are false or real. These are stances toward the same quoted phrase, not new senses.
